title: Don't lean on mortals
hookLine: don't rest your hopes on people who cannot save you (Sukhmani 14)

lines: HE'LL PUT IN A WORD FOR YOU.
cards: A friend said he'd put in a word for you. He knows the manager. It's basically done, he said.
So you stopped applying anywhere else. Two weeks, three weeks. Then a text: so sorry, it didn't work out, they went internal.

He meant well. He just couldn't carry what you'd put on him. It's easy to lean your whole weight on somebody like that, a friend, a boss, a parent, a partner, and feel the floor tilt when they can't hold it.

teach.h: TEK: THE PROP YOU LEAN ON.
teach.b: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: know that all reliance on mortals is in vain; the Giver is the One Lord alone. The key word is tek: a prop, a support, like a walking stick or a post you rest your back against.
Brithee means useless, in vain. So the human prop won't bear the weight. That could sound bleak, even cold.

Don't trust people? But Sikh life doesn't look like that at all. The tradition runs on people: the sangat, the company; the langar, cooked and served by volunteers; families who carry each other for generations.
Sukhmani itself, a few days back, told us to take shelter in the company of the good.

teach.h: NOT: HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH PEOPLE.
teach.b: So the stanza can't mean, have nothing to do with people. It's narrower and kinder. It's about the last weight, the final hope, the thing you'd collapse without.
People are limited, not because they're bad, but because they're people. They get sick, they forget, they move away, they die. Your friend couldn't control the manager.
When all your hope rests on one person, you've asked them to be something no human can be, and when they fail, you end up resenting them for being human.
Lean your final weight on the One, the stanza says, and something surprising happens.
You can love people without crushing them.
Your friend can be just a friend: a good one, a limited one, and that's enough.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the fourteenth ashtpadi's first stanza on the vain reliance on mortals, while Sikh life continues to rest heavily on sangat, family and community service.

o: a vow you keep at the gurdwara
a prop or support you lean on
a debt that you owe a friend

games.q: don't lean on mortals — tap the pairs.

s: this stanza tells Sikhs to have nothing to do with other people
Sikh life runs on sangat and langar; the stanza is about the final weight of hope.
tek means a prop or support you lean on
like a walking stick or a post at your back.
the stanza says people fail because they are bad
people are limited because they are people: they forget, fall ill, move, die.

games.q: a friend promised to get you the job, and it fell through. by the fourteenth ashtpadi, what's the lesson?
o: your final hope was resting on a human prop.
find a friend with better connections.
games.why: maanukh kee tek brithee: the human prop can't bear the final weight. the stanza points to the One, so the friend can be just a friend.

practice: Let your body lean into the chair, the wall or the floor, and notice what's holding you right now.

Then bring to mind one person you've been leaning on very hard, see them kindly as a person with limits, and gently take a little weight off them, letting it rest deeper, wherever you sense something steadier than any one person.
If you pray, rest it in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Tek, a prop, a support. Maanukh kee tek, the human prop, can't bear your final weight; Sukhmani says rest that weight in the One.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: tek, a prop or support, the thing one leans on.

carryVoice: Your line: lean on the one. Then people can just be people. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 14, stanza 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 281)
